p1c1.essay:
The first sentence already holds the book: a young man walks 'slowly, as though in hesitation.' Dostoevsky could have opened on an event. He opens on a man who is not sure he is going where he is going, and for the whole chapter we are not told what the errand is. It is 'that', 'a thing like that', the 'project', the 'hideous' dream, always in italics or inverted commas. I take the evasion to be Raskolnikov's before it is the author's. He cannot say the word to himself, so we get the thought from the outside only: a route counted in steps, an inventory of somebody's keys, a too-casual question about whether a sister is at home.

What strikes me most is how badly suited he is to whatever it is. He creeps past his landlady 'like a cat'. A drunk shouts at his hat and he clutches it 'tremulously'. Out in the street afterwards he calls his own heart filthy. Yet in between he is cool enough to register that the keys live in the right-hand pocket, all on one steel ring. The chapter keeps both men in view, the one who recoils and the one who takes notes, and declines to say which is real. The narrator, meanwhile, knows more about the hero than the hero does: he has come to regard the dream as 'an exploit to be attempted, although he still did not realise this himself.' That is a remarkable thing to be told on page three, that a decision can be made in a person without his being present for it.

Then there is the city. July, when everyone with money has left; plaster, scaffolding, dust, the stench from the 'pot-houses' (Garnett's period word for cheap drinking dens), and a man who has 'scarcely tasted food' for two days. Dostoevsky offers the medical reading quite fairly. A glass of beer and Raskolnikov himself decides it was all 'physical derangement'. I would not throw that explanation away, and neither does the novel; it just refuses to let it be the whole account, and the chapter's last word on his relief is that it too was 'not normal'.

One small thing to carry forward. The old woman's room is yellow: yellow paper, yellow wood, yellow frames, a fur cape 'yellow with age'. Watch that colour. It follows him home in [[p1c3]].

annotations.quote: I want to attempt a thing _like that_ and am frightened by these trifles
annotations.note: The first thing we hear him think, and the object is already missing. Garnett's underscores mark Dostoevsky's italics, and the italics do the work of a name he will not use. Notice too that he is not ashamed of the thing; he is ashamed of being frightened of his landlady.

annotations.quote: It’s because I chatter that I do nothing. Or perhaps it is that I chatter because I do nothing.
annotations.note: He turns the sentence round and cannot tell which way the cause runs. This is his habit of mind in miniature: every thought is immediately cross-examined by another, and the cross-examination becomes a substitute for doing anything.

annotations.quote: Not shame, however, but quite another feeling akin to terror had overtaken him.
annotations.note: A tall German hat, and it terrifies him, because it would be remembered. The narrator is careful to separate shame from fear here. A poor student ought to mind being laughed at; this one minds being noticed, which is a different kind of person to be.

annotations.quote: exactly seven hundred and thirty. He had counted them once when he had been lost in dreams.
annotations.note: My favourite detail in the chapter. He counted the steps while 'lost in dreams', so the dreaming and the measuring were the same activity. Whatever this plan is, it began as a fantasy that happened to keep very exact records.

annotations.quote: The bell gave a faint tinkle as though it were made of tin and not of copper.
annotations.note: A cheap, thin sound, and it 'seemed to remind him of something'. Dostoevsky rarely spends this long on a noise. Keep the note of that bell in your ear.

annotations.quote: Round her thin long neck, which looked like a hen’s leg, was knotted some sort of flannel rag
annotations.note: She is made almost conveniently repellent: oiled hair, malignant eyes, a neck like a hen's leg. It is worth asking who is doing the looking. The narrator has been inside Raskolnikov's head all chapter, and this portrait reads to me like something he needs her to be.

annotations.quote: “So the sun will shine like this _then_ too!”
annotations.note: Another italic standing in for a noun. The thought arrives 'as it were by chance', which is how the most important thoughts arrive in this book. And it is a strangely gentle one: he is imagining a future afternoon by its light.

annotations.quote: that’s worth knowing. Strong-boxes always have keys like that... but how degrading it all is.
annotations.note: Reconnaissance and revulsion in one breath, joined by three dots. He does not stop noting the keys because it is degrading; he notes them and finds it degrading. The two run side by side without cancelling.

annotations.quote: he had a dim foreboding that this happier frame of mind was also not normal.
annotations.note: The chapter has just offered a comfortable explanation, hunger and nerves, cured by beer. This sentence takes it back. If the dread was a symptom, so is the relief, and he half knows it.

links.why: His own room, described at last, turns out to share its wallpaper and its dimensions with the mood he carried here.
The book later circles back to tell how the 'dreams' of a month ago began; read it with this rehearsal in mind.
The retired clerk glimpsed in the last paragraph is about to take over the novel for a chapter.

p1c2.essay:
A novel that began inside one man's head now hands the floor to a stranger and lets him talk for twenty pages. I find that boldness easy to underrate. We have just been given a hero with a secret, and Dostoevsky makes him sit still and listen to a drunk. The reason, I think, is that Marmeladov's monologue is the first full statement of what the book is about, and it had to come from someone other than Raskolnikov, in a register Raskolnikov would never use.

The register first, since Garnett works hard at it. Marmeladov speaks the Russian of government offices gone to seed: 'forasmuch as', 'honoured sir', 'I make bold to inquire'. He is a titular counsellor, a low rung of the civil-service ladder, and the grand style is the verbal version of the single button he keeps fastened on his coat. It is funny, and the tavern laughs, and Dostoevsky lets it be funny. But listen to what the style carries. 'Poverty is not a vice', he says, but beggary is, because the beggar is 'swept out with a broom'. And twice, the phrase that I think is the centre of the chapter: a man 'must have somewhere to go'. Not money, not food. Somewhere to go, someone who will 'feel for him'.

It would be simple if he were only a victim, and the chapter will not allow it. He stole his wife's last roubles from her box. He is drinking, as he speaks, the thirty copecks his daughter gave him that morning. He tells the whole story to a room that 'know all about it already', and he tells it well, with pauses and refrains ('do you hear, do you hear?'), like a man who has performed it before. Most uncomfortable of all, he enjoys his abasement. 'I drink so that I may suffer twice as much.' Being dragged by the hair is 'a positive con-so-la-tion'. Dostoevsky is interested in this pleasure in suffering and does not explain it away; hold on to it, because Marmeladov is not the only person in the book who has it.

Then Sonia, who is not here. Everything we learn of her comes through her father, and he gives it in a handful of physical facts: a soft little voice, a kerchief, thirty roubles laid on a table 'in silence', a green shawl pulled over her face, shoulders shuddering. The 'yellow ticket' he mentions is the registration card the police issued to prostitutes in place of an ordinary passport, which is why she can no longer lodge with respectable people. What I admire is that the scene has no villain. Katerina Ivanovna says the unforgivable thing 'more to wound her than anything else', and then spends the evening on her knees kissing the girl's feet. Lebeziatnikov, the lodger with 'modern ideas', is the nearest the chapter comes to a target, and through him we first hear the new doctrine that 'compassion is forbidden nowadays by science itself'. It reaches us as tavern gossip, third-hand, from a drunk. That is a sly way to introduce the ideas of the 1860s into a novel that will take them very seriously.

The Last Judgment speech is usually read as the book's Christian keynote, and it is magnificent: the drunkards summoned last, the wise objecting, and the answer that they are received because 'not one of them believed himself to be worthy of this.' I believe he means it. I also notice that he is writing his own pardon, with the pot empty in front of him, and that the listeners go straight back to laughing. Dostoevsky gives us the vision and the reasons to distrust the visionary in the same breath, and does not tell us which to keep.

And Raskolnikov? He says about six sentences. But watch his hands and then his head. He leaves his coppers on the window sill, without being seen. On the stairs he thinks it 'a stupid thing', sneers at the family for making the most of Sonia, and arrives at 'Man grows used to everything, the scoundrel!' Then comes a last paragraph I have read many times and still find slippery: what if man is not a scoundrel, 'then all the rest is prejudice' and 'there are no barriers'. I am not sure the logic holds. What I am sure of is the word 'barriers', and that he reached for it while walking home from that room.

annotations.quote: He pounced upon Raskolnikov as greedily as though he too had not spoken to a soul for a month.
annotations.note: 'He too.' The narrator quietly pairs them: two men who have been shut up with one thought for a month. Marmeladov picks Raskolnikov out of the room because he reads 'some trouble of mind' in his face, and he is not wrong.

annotations.quote: compassion is forbidden nowadays by science itself, and that that’s what is done now in England, where there is political economy.
annotations.note: The joke is on Lebeziatnikov, but the target is real: the utilitarian economics, Mill and his Russian admirers, that was fashionable among the young in the 1860s. Note how the idea first enters the novel, garbled and second-hand. It will come back in better clothes.

annotations.quote: For every man must have somewhere to go.
annotations.note: The plainest sentence in the speech, and the one that lasts. He is explaining why a man asks for a loan he knows will be refused. It is about asking, not about getting. Raskolnikov will hear this again in his own head in [[p1c4]].

annotations.quote: I drink so that I may suffer twice as much!
annotations.note: Not to forget, which is what drinkers are supposed to say. He drinks to feel it more. I think Dostoevsky means this literally, as a description of a real appetite, and the novel keeps returning to people who seek out their own punishment.

annotations.quote: We stopped at Cyrus of Persia.
annotations.note: A whole failed education in five words. He tried to teach his daughter universal history, the books ran out, and they never got past the sixth century B.C. It is the funniest line in the chapter and it is also the measure of what Sonia was given to face the world with.

annotations.quote: she laid thirty roubles on the table before her in silence.
annotations.note: Thirty, and silver roubles are the coin of the scene. The echo of the thirty pieces is surely meant, but turned inside out: here the one who is sold is the one who brings the money. A few pages on it shrinks to thirty copecks, her last, for his drink.

annotations.quote: But it hurts more, it hurts more when they don’t blame!
annotations.note: He can bear his wife pulling his hair; he says he needs it. What he cannot bear is his daughter looking at him and saying nothing. Forgiveness as the harder thing to receive than punishment: file that away.

annotations.quote: that not one of them believed himself to be worthy of this.
annotations.note: The hinge of the sermon. The drunkards are let in not for any merit but because they never thought they had one, and the 'wise' are the ones who object. A novel that began with a clever young man alone with his ideas gives its first great speech to a drunk, and the speech ends by putting cleverness in the dock.

annotations.quote: to lay them unnoticed on the window. Afterwards on the stairs, he changed his mind and would have gone back.
annotations.note: The first thing we see him do for another person, and he does it in secret and regrets it within a flight of stairs. The hand gives before the mind has been consulted; then the mind arrives and calls it stupid. Watch for this sequence again.

annotations.quote: Man grows used to everything, the scoundrel!
annotations.note: He is talking about the family living on Sonia, and the contempt is partly a defence against what he has just felt. But it is also a fair description of what the chapter showed: people weeping over a thing and then building a household budget on it.

links.why: Marmeladov's 'nowhere to turn' comes back to Raskolnikov the next afternoon, and Sonia's name with it.
The two tavern-goers were set side by side in the last lines there: one man who chatters and does nothing, another who is about to out-chatter him.
Sonia, who exists here only as her father's story, is eventually allowed to speak for herself; this is the chapter to compare with his account.

p1c3.essay:
After the tavern, the cupboard. We finally see Raskolnikov's room, and it is the old woman's room gone to ruin: 'dusty yellow paper peeling off the walls', a ceiling he could knock his head on, a sofa for a bed. He likes it this way, 'like a tortoise in its shell'. Into this comes Nastasya with her cracked teapot and yesterday's cabbage soup, the only person so far who simply laughs at him. Her questions are the right ones. What are you doing? 'I am thinking.' Have you made much money by it? I am grateful to Dostoevsky for her, because without that silent shaking laughter the book would have no outside to its hero's head.

Then the letter, which Garnett prints as it should be printed, in great unbroken blocks, a mother talking without drawing breath. It is one of the best pieces of indirect characterisation I know. Pulcheria Alexandrovna cannot say a reassuring thing about her daughter's suitor without taking half of it back: he is 'thoroughly estimable' but 'a little morose and somewhat conceited'; he 'seems to be good-natured'; it 'did strike me as somewhat rude'. She reports his theory about marrying a poor girl so that the wife will see her husband 'as her benefactor', and then hurries to say she has probably misremembered the wording. She knows. The letter is an attempt to talk herself out of knowing, written to the one reader she cannot fool.

It is also, and this is easy to miss under the feeling, a set of accounts. A pension of a hundred and twenty roubles a year. Fifteen borrowed against it. Sixty sent last year, which turn out to have come from an advance on Dounia's wages, the debt that kept her in that house. Her son learns in one paragraph that his studies have been paid for with his sister's humiliation, and that a second and larger payment is being arranged. 'You are our all, our one hope, our one stay' is pure love, and it lands on him like a weight.

There is comedy too, and I would not skip it: Marfa Petrovna touring the town to read Dounia's letter aloud, by appointment, house by house. Dostoevsky trained on Dickens and Gogol and it shows.

What the chapter does not do is comment. We heard last night, in [[p1c2]], about a daughter who went out one evening for her family's sake. Nobody here draws the line between that story and this one. Raskolnikov kisses the envelope, weeps, and finishes with 'a bitter, wrathful and malignant smile'. The line gets drawn in [[p1c4]].

annotations.quote: It was a tiny cupboard of a room about six paces in length.
annotations.note: The narrator called it a cupboard on the first page; by the end of this chapter it is 'a cupboard or a box'. Dostoevsky wants us to feel thought being shaped by a ceiling. Whether a room can be blamed for an idea is a question the novel asks more than once.

annotations.quote: “I am thinking,” he answered seriously after a pause.
annotations.note: He means it, and that is what makes Nastasya laugh until she feels ill. To her, thinking is not work. To him it has become the only work, a month of it, lying on a sofa. Both of them are right, which is the trouble.

annotations.quote: And you want to get a fortune all at once?
annotations.note: A peasant woman's teasing, and it goes in like a needle. 'He looked at her strangely' and answers 'firmly' that yes, he does. She has stumbled on the shape of his thought, all at once rather than copeck by copeck, and frightened herself.

annotations.quote: he lifted it quickly to his lips and kissed it
annotations.note: Only when he is alone. This is the same man who looked at the pawnbroker's keys last night, and Dostoevsky wants both pictures in our heads. Compare this gesture with the expression on his face when he has finished reading.

annotations.quote: you are all we have to look to, Dounia and I, you are our all, our one hope, our one stay.
annotations.note: Said in the first few lines, before any news. Read as love it is touching. Read as a job description, by a young man with no boots who has left the university, it is crushing. The letter returns to the phrase at its close, as if to make sure.

annotations.quote: and even allowed them to take copies of it--which I must say I think was superfluous.
annotations.note: The mother's mildness is the comedy. A whole town queues to hear a governess's private letter read aloud, people take offence at the order of visits, and the strongest word she permits herself is 'superfluous'. That same mildness is what she will bring to judging the suitor.

annotations.quote: it is better for a wife to look upon her husband as her benefactor.
annotations.note: The whole man in a clause. He wants a wife who is poor so that she will be grateful, and he says so at his second visit. The mother records it faithfully and then spends four sentences apologising for him. Her son will not need the apology explained.

annotations.quote: that is to say, he has taken upon himself the conveyance of our bags and big trunk
annotations.note: 'Part of the expenses' turns out, on inspection, to mean the luggage. She writes it as a kindness. The women will go ninety versts by cart and then third class. It is the kind of detail a reader slides over and a son does not.

annotations.quote: Do you still say your prayers, Rodya, and believe in the mercy of our Creator and our Redeemer?
annotations.note: Left for the very end, after the money and the marriage, the question she is most afraid to ask. 'The new spirit of infidelity that is abroad' is her name for the ideas we heard mangled in the tavern. She does not wait for an answer; she says she will pray.

annotations.quote: a bitter, wrathful and malignant smile was on his lips.
annotations.note: Tears while reading, this when he finishes. Garnett uses 'malignant' for the pawnbroker's eyes, for his laugh after leaving the Marmeladovs, and now here. The word is doing a lot of travelling between people who are supposed to be nothing alike.

links.why: He goes straight out and rereads the letter aloud to himself, phrase by phrase, and it is a very different document in his mouth.
Set the mother's account of Dounia beside Marmeladov's account of Sonia: two families, two daughters, two sums of money.
The suitor the letter describes so anxiously comes to Petersburg, as promised; test the mother's portrait against the man.

p1c4.essay:
Raskolnikov reads his mother's letter the way a prosecutor reads a deposition. He has it by heart after one reading and throws its phrases back: 'seems to be kind', 'our most rising generation', 'Dounia can put up with a great deal'. He is a formidable close reader, and almost everything he finds is really there. The luggage that costs the fiancé nothing. The mother who has already guessed she will not be welcome in the married household. The little word 'seems', which he cannot leave alone. If you felt in [[p1c3]] that the letter was protesting too much, this is the pleasure of being told you were right.

But look at how he reads. He does not quote accurately. The letter says Dounia 'was vexed'; he makes it 'answered her angrily'. He supplies whole speeches for both women. And the tone is a kind of furious relish: 'Splendid! splendid!' The narrator, who misses nothing, says a little later that he tortured himself with these questions 'finding a kind of enjoyment in it'. We heard about that enjoyment last night from a man being dragged by his hair. I do not think Dostoevsky is saying the two are the same. He is saying the taste is not confined to drunkards.

The thought he arrives at is the one the last chapter left hanging. His sister is selling herself, lawfully, for him, and so 'Sonia's life is no worse than life with Mr. Luzhin.' A girl he has never seen, known only from a tavern monologue, has become a category in his mind: 'the eternal victim so long as the world lasts.' It is a hard, clear, unsentimental equation, and it is to his credit that he then turns it on himself. The voice changes to the second person: 'what are you going to do to prevent it? ... You are living upon them.' 'Future millionaire Zeus' is his own sneer at his own promises. He has nothing to offer in place of Luzhin. And into that gap, expected, 'felt beforehand', comes yesterday's thought, the one from [[p1c1]] that still has no name, now in 'a new menacing and quite unfamiliar shape'. Notice what Dostoevsky has done with three chapters. He showed us the idea first, as a fantasy with nothing behind it. Only afterwards did he supply Marmeladov and the letter. The pressure arrives after the plan, not before, and I think that order is deliberate and unsettling. It is harder to say the circumstances caused the thought when the thought was there waiting for them.

Then the book does something I love: it tests the theorist at once, on a real case. A drunk girl of fifteen or sixteen on a bench, a fat dandy hovering. Raskolnikov acts without thinking and acts well. He shouts 'Svidrigaïlov!' at a total stranger, the name from the letter already serving him as a common noun for a type. He reads the torn dress like a detective, enlists the policeman, hands over twenty copecks. And then 'something seemed to sting' him and he calls it all off: 'Let him amuse himself.' The reversal takes one line. I find it the most frightening moment so far, more than anything on the pawnbroker's stairs, because we watch a decent impulse being revoked by an idea. It is the coppers on the Marmeladovs' window again, only faster and out loud. His name has the Russian word for schism, raskol, inside it, and here the split is visible.

The idea that does the revoking is 'percentage'. Social statisticians of the day, Quetelet above all, had shown that a steady proportion of any population turns each year to crime or to the streets, and the radical journals took this as proof that such things were laws of nature and nobody's fault. Raskolnikov is savage about it: 'so scientific, so consolatory'. Yet he has just behaved exactly as the statistic recommends. He despises the argument and obeys it. Only the thought of Dounia as 'one of the percentage' breaks the trance.

And then, oddly, Razumihin. He discovers he was walking to see a friend and cannot think why. The portrait that follows reads like a digression and is nothing of the kind. Here is a student just as poor, also forced out of the university, who spent a winter without lighting his stove and declared he slept better for it. His name is built on razum, good sense. Dostoevsky sets him down quietly at the end of the chapter as a standing objection: the same garret, the same hunger, and no fearful question at all.

annotations.quote: Was it all put into _words_, or did both understand that they had the same thing at heart
annotations.note: He wants to know whether mother and sister said the bargain aloud or only understood each other. It is a sharp question about how families manage sacrifice. It is also asked by a man who has spent a month not putting his own intention into words.

annotations.quote: Sonia, Sonia Marmeladov, the eternal victim so long as the world lasts.
annotations.note: He has never met her. One evening's hearsay and she has become an emblem, and a rather grand one. I would keep a little distance from the phrase: it is Raskolnikov's way of thinking, turning a person into a principle, and the book is interested in what that habit costs.

annotations.quote: oh, future millionaire Zeus who would arrange their lives for them?
annotations.note: The self-mockery is exact. He forbids the marriage like a god handing down a decree and in the next breath remembers he lives on their borrowed roubles. 'I want a fortune', he told Nastasya this morning; here is why, and here is how far he is from it.

annotations.quote: So he tortured himself, fretting himself with such questions, and finding a kind of enjoyment in it.
annotations.note: The narrator steps back from the monologue to tell us something Raskolnikov would not say of himself. Set it beside Marmeladov's 'I drink so that I may suffer twice as much' in [[p1c2]]. The clever student and the ruined clerk share an appetite.

annotations.quote: it had taken a new menacing and quite unfamiliar shape, and he suddenly became aware of this himself
annotations.note: In the first chapter the narrator told us the dream had become a project 'although he still did not realise this himself'. Now he realises. The thing still has no name on the page, but its status has changed, and what changed it was a letter full of love.

annotations.quote: “Hey! You Svidrigaïlov! What do you want here?”
annotations.note: The dandy has never heard the name. Raskolnikov has just had it from his mother's letter as the name of the man who hounded his sister, and it is already his word for any man circling a defenceless girl. He is fighting the boulevard stranger for Dounia's sake, and half knows it.

annotations.quote: Let them be! What is it to do with you? Let her go! Let him amuse himself.
annotations.note: A complete reversal inside a minute, and he laughs as he says it. Nothing outside him has changed: the girl is still walking, the man still following. Something he thought overruled something he felt. The policeman decides he is mad, which is the kinder reading.

annotations.quote: How did I dare to give him twenty copecks? Were they mine?
annotations.note: A strange scruple, and a revealing one. The money came from his mother, raised on her pension, so in his own eyes he has no right even to be generous with it. Having nothing of his own has reached the point where it forbids him to do good.

annotations.quote: Once you’ve said ‘percentage’ there’s nothing more to worry about.
annotations.note: His contempt for the word is real. Statistics turn a ruined girl into a figure in a column, and the figure soothes. What makes the passage bite is that he is describing the anaesthetic while it is working on him, and it stops working only when he puts his sister's name in the column.

annotations.quote: And though Razumihin noticed him, he passed him by, as he did not want to annoy him.
annotations.note: The last sentence of the portrait, and the one that tells us most about the friend. He saw Raskolnikov cross the street to avoid him and let him do it, out of tact. That is a great deal of delicacy in a man reputed to floor policemen.

links.why: Keep the letter open beside this chapter and check his quotations against it; where he misquotes is as telling as where he is right.
Marmeladov's question about having 'nowhere to turn' and his remarks on what 'smartness' costs are both recalled here word for word.
The walk towards Razumihin, and the argument he is having with himself, continue without a break.
